hook: Flip a coin ten times and you might get seven heads. Is the coin unfair, or was that luck? Psychologists face the same question with every study: two groups always differ a little, even when the treatment does nothing. Statistical significance is how they decide whether a difference is bigger than luck alone would usually produce.

prereq.q: Two classes have the same mean score, 75, but Class B has a much larger standard deviation. What does that mean?
options: Class B’s scores are more spread out
Class B scored higher on average
prereq.why: A larger standard deviation means the scores are more spread out around the mean.

prereq.q: Researchers draw 300 names at random from a list of every student in a state. What does this random sampling allow?
options: Generalizing the results to the state’s students
prereq.why: Random sampling makes a representative sample likely, so results can generalize to the population.

figure.caption: A small and a large effect size: how far apart two groups’ scores are.

chain.effect: researchers need to judge whether a difference is bigger than chance usually produces

chain.cause: Inferential statistics estimate how likely a difference this large would be by chance alone
chain.effect: below 5% ($p < .05$), the result is called statistically significant

chain.cause: A very large sample makes even tiny differences unlikely to be chance
chain.effect: a significant result can still be small, so effect size is reported to say how big it is

ideas: Descriptive statistics summarize a sample; inferential statistics use the sample to draw conclusions about the population.
Statistically significant ($p < .05$): a difference this large would be unlikely if only chance were at work. Not significant: the difference could plausibly be chance.
Effect size says how big the difference or relationship is. Significance is not size: big samples make small effects significant.
Always read a result for its groups: which group was higher, by how much, whether it was significant, and how large the effect was.

misconception.wrong: "Statistically significant" means the effect is large or important, and "not significant" proves there is no effect.
misconception.right: Significant only means unlikely to be chance; the size comes from the effect size. Not significant means chance cannot be ruled out, which is not proof of no effect, especially in a small study.

summary: Inferential statistics let researchers judge whether a sample’s result reflects the population. A statistically significant difference ($p < .05$) is unlikely to be due to chance alone; a difference that is not significant could plausibly be chance. Significance does not measure size: effect size tells how big a difference is, and with very large samples even tiny effects can be significant.
